rental-property-calculator.quickAnswer: Effective rent = rent x (1 - vacancy); cash flow = effective rent - expenses - mortgage; cap rate = NOI / price. Example: a 3,000,000 property renting at 32,000 per month with 5% vacancy, 6,000 monthly expenses, 25% down, and a 9% 15-year loan has 30,400 effective rent, a 22,821 mortgage, 1,579 monthly cash flow, a 9.76% cap rate, and 2.53% cash-on-cash. The 1% rule passes at 1.07%.

rental-property-calculator.formula:
Effective rent = Rent x (1 - Vacancy % / 100).
Monthly cash flow = Effective rent - Expenses - Mortgage payment.
Cap rate = (Effective rent - Expenses) x 12 / Price x 100.
Cash-on-cash = Monthly cash flow x 12 / Down payment x 100.
1% rule = Rent / Price x 100 (pass at 1.0 or more).
Example: 30,400 - 6,000 - 22,821 = 1,579 cash flow; 292,800 / 3,000,000 = 9.76% cap.
benefits: Models vacancy honestly instead of pretending the flat is always full.

faqs.a: A screening rule: monthly rent should be at least 1% of the purchase price. A 3,000,000 property should rent for 30,000 or more. It is a filter, not a valuation: passing properties deserve deeper analysis, failing ones are usually skipped.

faqs.q: What vacancy rate should I assume?
faqs.a: Five to 8% (about one month empty per year) suits stable markets; use 10% or more for volatile areas, student housing, or luxury segments. Check local listings: long vacancy ads signal a soft market.

faqs.q: Why is cash-on-cash lower than the cap rate?
faqs.a: Because leverage costs money. The cap rate ignores your loan; cash-on-cash subtracts the mortgage payment. When the loan rate exceeds the cap rate, leverage drags your cash return below the property's own yield, which is called negative leverage.

faqs.q: Should I buy for cash flow or appreciation?
faqs.a: Cash flow pays you now and survives flat markets; appreciation pays later and needs the market's help. Most landlords prefer cash flow first, treating appreciation as a bonus, because you cannot pay bills with unrealized gains.

faqs.q: What expenses do new landlords forget?
faqs.a: Vacancy allowance, routine maintenance (budget 1% of value per year), property management fees, insurance, property tax, and leasing commissions. Together they routinely reach 30 to 45% of gross rent.

faqs.q: How is this different from the real estate calculators?
faqs.a: This one is rental-specific: vacancy modeling, the 1% rule, and rental ROI. The real estate calculator is the quick cash-flow screen, and the investment calculator adds cap rate, GRM, and DSCR for financed deals.

labels.onePass: 1% rule passes: rent is at least 1% of the price.
labels.oneFail: 1% rule fails: rent is below 1% of the price, cash flow will be tight.
